questions: Do you have episodes of weakness or inability to move that come and go?
Do these episodes occur only when someone is watching or examining you?
Do you have numbness or altered sensation?
Have you ever lost consciousness during an episode?
Do you have difficulty speaking or swallowing?
Do you have double vision or drooping eyelids that worsen with activity?
Do you have a history of seizures?
Do you have anxiety, depression, or significant psychological stress?
Does your speech become strained or “spasmodic” mainly when you try to speak in sentences?
Is your voice noticeably better when whispering or singing?
Do you have involuntary jerking or abnormal posturing of your neck, face, jaw, or limbs?
Did the speech problem begin suddenly?
Do you experience abnormal breathing or noisy breathing when speaking?
Are the involuntary movements most prominent in your face, jaw, or tongue?
Are they lessened by touching your face or by another “sensory trick”?
Can you temporarily suppress the movements when asked?
Do the movements worsen with speaking or other voluntary actions?
Do you take, or have you previously taken, antipsychotic or anti-nausea medications such as haloperidol, risperidone, metoclopramide, or prochlorperazine?
Does anyone in your biological family have similar involuntary movements or an early neurodegenerative disorder?
Do you have progressive problems with coordination, memory, or personality?
Do the involuntary movements disappear completely when you are asleep?
Do they vary substantially from one moment to the next?
Are the movements absent when you are distracted by a complex mental task?
Did the movements and speech problem begin after an injury, illness, or major stressful event?
Have brain MRI or other neurological tests previously shown no structural abnormality?
Did the abnormal movements begin before the age of 26?
Did the movements start in one limb and then spread to other body regions?
Have the movements progressively worsened over time?
Do you have sustained twisting or abnormal postures of the neck, trunk, arms, or legs?
Do you have tremor in addition to the abnormal postures?
Have you ever had a good response to levodopa?
Have you had symptoms such as difficulty with eye movements, rigidity, or slowed movement?
orders: Bedside cranial-nerve examination focused on bulbar function: sustained counting aloud, repetition of lingual and labial phrases, inspection of palate elevation while saying “ah,” tongue protrusion and side-to-side movement, and bilateral gag-reflex testing.
Formal speech-and-swallow evaluation with water swallow test.

Bedside cranial-nerve examination focused on bulbar function: sustained counting aloud, repetition of lingual and labial phrases, inspection of palate elevation while saying “ah,” tongue protrusion and side-to-side movement, and bilateral gag-reflex testing.
Formal speech-and-swallow evaluation with water swallow test.

Bedside movement-disorder examination assessing variability, distractibility with mental and contralateral motor tasks, entrainment of any tremor or rhythmic movement, suggestibility, and consistency across repeated voluntary maneuvers.
Video laryngoscopy during sustained vowel, conversational speech, whispering, and singing to assess for laryngeal dystonia or functional dysphonia.
MRI of the brain with and without contrast, including basal-ganglia sequences.
Serum ceruloplasmin and serum copper, 24-hour urinary copper, liver-function tests, and slit-lamp examination for Kayser–Fleischer rings.
Electromyography of the affected muscles during rest, voluntary contraction, and the abnormal postures, assessing for dystonic co-contraction.
Comprehensive genetic testing for isolated dystonia, including sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis of TOR1A, THAP1, GNAL, and other established primary-dystonia genes.
Surface EMG of the involved muscles during rest, voluntary movement, and the sustained abnormal postures to document dystonic co-contraction.
served: needle EMG of the affected muscles
